items.stem: A university already has a web API that returns course data as JSON. It now wants an Android app that shows the same courses. What does the Android app need from the backend?

options.text: Nothing new. The app can call the same URLs and show the JSON its own way
options.feedback: The API returns the same data whatever client calls it. Any client that can send HTTP requests and read JSON can use it.

options.text: A separate backend for Android, because Android apps cannot read JSON
options.feedback: Android apps read JSON without difficulty. A second backend would also mean two copies of the data and the business rules.

options.text: The web page's HTML, shown inside the app in a built-in browser
options.feedback: HTML contains layout decisions for a browser. A native app is built to draw its own screens from the data.

items.stem: A system returns finished HTML tables from its server. The university wants an iOS app that shows the same course list. What is the main difficulty?

options.text: The data is mixed with layout, so someone must scrape the HTML or build an API.
options.feedback: There is no separate data layer to call. Scraping breaks whenever the page layout changes, so building an API means pulling the logic out of the page-generating code.

options.text: iOS apps cannot open a connection to a server that returns HTML pages.
options.feedback: Any app can connect to the server. The problem is that the response is built for a browser and not for another program.

options.text: The server does not hold enough data to fill a mobile app's screens.
options.feedback: The data is the same. It is the form of the response that makes the app hard to build.

items.stem: Your team adds a new optional field to an API response and removes nothing. What happens to people who still run an old version of the app?

options.text: Nothing breaks. The old app ignores the field it does not know
options.feedback: This is an additive change. Old clients read the fields they expect and skip the rest.

options.text: The old app crashes until the user updates to the new version
options.feedback: A crash would happen if a field the app expects had been renamed or removed. Adding a field removes nothing that the app needs.

options.text: The old app shows the new field automatically without an update
options.feedback: An app can only show fields its code knows about. The new field appears after the user updates.

items.stem: You rename the field `slots` to `seats` and ship the change. Seven days later, who is most likely to see errors?

options.text: Mobile users who have not updated their app
options.feedback: Web users get new code on their next reload, but mobile users must update through the store, and many wait weeks. Old app copies still ask for `slots`.

options.text: Web users, because browsers cache old pages
options.feedback: Web code updates on the next reload, so web users are the first group to recover.

options.text: Nobody, because the server was updated
options.feedback: The server now sends `seats`, but old app copies still look for `slots` and fail.

items.try: In the step "Change an API", select Breaking, move the slider to 7 days, and read the percentage on each platform's bar.
